newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU, U.S. reach infotech agreement, hail huge advance.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. reach infotech agreement, hail huge advance.

text.p: Europe announced agreement on Thursday with the United States to scrap tariffs on billions of dollars of information technology trade by the year 2000 and hailed the pact as one of the biggest steps toward global free commerce.

"The basis of what we have agreed with the United States provides for a deal on ITA (information technology agreement) which will be a huge advance for the world economy," European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference.

The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- had set the pact as a key target to declaring this week's first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) a real success.
"This is extraordinarily positive," U.S. spokesman Jay Ziegler told reporters.

The breakthrough came when Brittan won endorsement of the 15-member European Union Council for an outline agreement hammered out with the United States after three days of intense, late-night talks at the December 9-13 WTO meeting in Singapore.
The council met after an early morning briefing between Brittan and Acting U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky.
Barshefksy had earlier expressed doubts about European commitment to the ITA accord.
The European Council endorsement clears a major obstacle for a world agreement by the Friday close of the WTO meeting.

The council mandated Brittan to seek broader support from other countries, many of them Asia's booming tiger economies, for the pact to eliminate worldwide tariffs in the $600 billion infotech sector by the turn of the century.

"This is the biggest trade step forward, if it is completed today, that has happened since the end of the Uruguay Round," Brittan said, referring to the largest set of measures ever adopted to liberalise world trade and completed in 1993.
Brittan said the final agreement still depended on enough countries -- those representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector -- joining the pact by March 15, 1997.

"Clearly, both Europe and the United States made it clear that this is not a bilateral agreement. It's meant to be agreement covering the countries in the world most involved in this whole area of activity," Brittan said.
Brittan said the 90 percent was not "a rigid barrier", although U.S. officials stressed that it was essential.

"We have had to work very hard to get to this point," Ziegler said. "Now the critical objective is to meet the 90 percent product coverage threshold, because if we don't do that the agreement doesn't take effect."
Some Asian members have already indicated support for the deal, but want flexibility over the timing of the tariff cuts.

Compromise between the United States and the EU had resulted in a deal that would cover the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.

The United States, whose high-tech firms would likely profit most from the ITA, has taken the lead in the push to forge a pact. Japan, also a huge player in the fast-growing sector, has backed the drive strongly.
The EU had been seeking to win compensation for scrapping its infotech tariffs, which are the highest among the Big Four.
